Route & site selection · South Africa

Route and servitude baselines for new transmission lines

For every alternative alignment, how many structures stand inside the future servitude and around it, where the slopes, drainage crossings and flood-prone stretches are, and what the land looked like before. Then, once the route is fixed, a dated register of what stands on it before servitude negotiations start. For utilities, independent transmission bidders, IPPs and the consultancies working for them. A person reviews every result.

Used in: Power & utilities · Renewables · Project finance & ESIA

Send us your route options Power lines in South Africa

Why the land question comes first

Servitude acquisition is a named risk in the national plan

TDP 2024

The national plan

About 14,494 km of new lines and 210 transformers for 2025 to 2034. The plan lists “delays in obtaining environmental authorisations, servitude acquisitions, and other statutory approvals” among its risks, and records a 400 kV line delayed by servitude acquisition (TDP 2024).

ITP Phase 1

Independent transmission

The request for qualification launched on 31 July 2025 and drew 17 responses; seven bidders were prequalified on 15 December 2025. The draft request for proposals goes to them, and the final one is expected in the 2026/27 financial year (DBSA).

GN 2313

Corridors without authorisation

Compliant lines inside the strategic transmission corridors are excluded from environmental authorisation under the power-line standard (GN 2313, 27 July 2022). The land baseline has to come from somewhere else, and earlier.

Renewable projects add their own lines: the three REIPPPP Bid Window 7 announcements between December 2024 and December 2025 named preferred bidders for 3,940 MW, and each project needs its grid connection and the servitude for it. See renewables and grid connections.

Compare alignments

Every option, measured the same way

We buffer each alternative alignment at the servitude width you expect and at a wider screening band, and count the structures inside each, stretch by stretch. The same rules apply to every option, so the numbers are comparable: which alignment crosses the fewest structures, where each one runs through dense settlement, and which stretches would need the most negotiation.

Alongside the counts, each option is screened for what makes a route expensive to build and maintain: steep and erosion-prone stretches and drainage crossings from elevation data, stretches in historically flooded or low-lying ground, and the land cover along the way. Where a parcel is contested, the imagery history shows roughly when it was built on or cleared.

The comparison is an input to route selection, not the decision. It does not promise that any option avoids resettlement, and the engineering, environmental and social assessments stay with your teams and consultants.

For each option

Measure From
Structures inside the servitude width Reviewed structure register
Structures in the wider band Reviewed structure register
Stretches rated high for encroachment density 500 m count rule
Estimated households, on request Structure counts and stated assumptions
Steep and erosion-prone stretches Copernicus DEM, drone models where flown
Drainage crossings and flood exposure Elevation data and past satellite water records
Land cover ESA WorldCover and Copernicus Sentinel

Once the route is fixed

A dated register before servitude negotiations start

When the alignment is chosen, we produce a dated register of the structures on it: each with an ID, coordinates, distance to the centreline, band and, where scoped, a reviewer’s category such as main building, outbuilding, livestock enclosure or under construction. Categories describe what the imagery shows; they do not establish use, ownership or value, and compensation needs ground verification.

Each landowner conversation can then start from the same dated list. During negotiations, the route is re-surveyed on a schedule you set, and new structures are flagged and confirmed by a reviewer.

For lender-financed lines

Where DFIs or Equator Principles banks finance a line or an IPP, IFC Performance Standard 5 applies. Our dated register supports your census and asset inventory and the IFC Performance Standard 5 cut-off-date records; it does not replace the census, and the cut-off date comes from your resettlement process.

Resettlement cut-off-date baselines

The law around acquisition

Servitudes, surveys and expropriation

Servitude diagrams

Surveys for registrable diagrams are reserved to professional land surveyors (Geomatics Profession Act, s13(2)(b)), and a diagram needs Surveyor-General approval (Land Survey Act 8 of 1997). Our registers show the surveyor what stands on the strip; they do not replace the survey.

Expropriation

The Expropriation Act 13 of 2024 is not yet implemented: the Minister told Parliament on 19 December 2025 that it faces constitutional challenges and that the Expropriation Act 63 of 1975 remains applicable (PMG).

Environmental authorisation

Where a line still needs authorisation, it runs under NEMA and the EIA Regulations 2014, as amended, with a registered environmental assessment practitioner. We supply counts and layers for the practitioner’s own maps and reports.

What you receive

Files your route, land and E&S teams can use

  • A comparison table for each alignment: structures by band, density ratings, terrain, drainage and flood screening, land cover
  • Maps of each option with the structures coloured by band
  • Imagery history for contested parcels, with the dates of the scenes used
  • Once the route is fixed, a dated structure register with IDs, coordinates and, where scoped, reviewer categories
  • Estimated households with the assumptions stated, on request
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

The comparison works the same way for pipelines, roads and connection lines. More on the method in route and site selection and the methodology.

Frequently asked questions

Is this the alternatives assessment for our environmental authorisation?

No. It is an input to route selection and to the environmental practitioner’s work, not a full alternatives assessment. It gives each option comparable counts and screening results; the assessment, its criteria and its conclusions stay with your EAP and engineers.

Can you tell us how many people each route affects?

We report structures, and on request estimated households derived from them, with the persons-per-household assumptions set out in the report. They are estimates for planning consultation and budgets, not a census, and they never replace the socio-economic survey.

Can you work to a bid timetable?

We agree the schedule in the proposal, section by section, and tell you at the start what the imagery for your area allows. Archive coverage, cloud and, for any drone work, permits set the pace, so we do not promise turnaround in advance of scoping.

Will the register stand up in servitude negotiations?

It is a dated, reviewed record of what stood on the route on the imagery date, with each structure located and measured to the line. It supports your landowner engagement, valuation and legal processes. It is not a cadastral survey. The servitude diagram is the work of a professional land surveyor.

Do you keep bidders' routes confidential?

Yes. Route options and results go only to the contacts you name, and we never publish a client’s routes, imagery or results without written permission.

Send us your route options

Each alternative as a line file (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile or GeoPackage), the servitude width you expect and any wider band to screen. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
